title: Name the feeling to tame it
description: A feeling with a precise name is easier to carry than a fog of “bad”; putting words to emotions is a small, learnable skill.

body.heading: Fog is harder than weather
paragraphs: “I feel awful” is a hard state to respond to, because it contains no instructions. But feelings become more manageable when they get specific: I feel embarrassed about the meeting, and angry underneath, and tired underneath that. Each named layer suggests something different — an apology, a boundary, a nap.
Naming does not make a feeling vanish. It makes it legible. A legible problem is one you can hold at arm’s length and look at, instead of being inside it like weather.

body.heading: Build a slightly bigger vocabulary
paragraphs: Start with the broad families — anger, sadness, fear, shame, joy — and practise narrowing by one step: not just angry, but frustrated, or disrespected, or rushed. Not just sad, but lonely, or disappointed, or homesick. The right word often brings a small physical sense of “yes, that one.”
A written feelings list or wheel can help at first; there is no exam. You are not labelling for a therapist or a diary. You are giving your own mind better handles for its own weather.

body.heading: Say it in the first person, in the present
paragraphs: A useful format: “Right now, I notice I feel ___ because ___ matters to me.” The “I notice” matters — it turns you into the observer of the feeling rather than its hostage — and the “because” connects the feeling to a value, which is usually where the useful action lives.
Feelings named this way often lose a size within minutes. What remains is frequently a practical problem wearing emotional clothes, and practical problems are the kind we know how to work on.

takeaway: When the feeling is a fog, give it a name — precision is a form of kindness to yourself.
